b: Louise Kennedy’s Stations, Daisy Johnson’s Long Wave, and Tom Drury’s West of Loveland all feature among the best reviewed fiction titles of the month.
Brought to you by Book Marks, Lit Hub’s home for book reviews.

“Extraordinary—and indeed bittersweet … There’s a lived-in circumspection to Kennedy’s work … Kennedy has earned a spot alongside contemporary Irish greats such as Eimear McBride and Sally Rooney, authors whose next project I’ll race to read, whatever they choose to write about.”

“Perhaps her strongest work yet … Johnson’s talent has always lain in her ability to combine vivid, poetic imagery that could have been wrenched from a myth or fairytale with writing that remains grounded in an almost mundane truthfulness … Johnson’s command of language is simply stunning … How the plot of Long Wave resolves is almost beside the point—and what a joy it is to read a writer who so confidently prioritizes character and language above gimmick or twist.”

3. West of Loveland by Tom Drury
(Grove)

6 Rave • 1 Positive

“Richly imagined … The novel’s measured pacing and cumulative power yield a deeply humane meditation on fate, belonging, and the unseen threads that connect seemingly ordinary lives.”

4. No Such Thing As Monday by Siân Hughes
(Henry Holt)

5 Rave • 2 Positive • 1 Mixed
Read an excerpt from No Such Thing As Monday here

“Fractious and darkly funny … Against almost every indication I’ve given you so far, this ouroboros of ongoing traumas somehow manages not to be head-smashingly bleak. Steffie is one of those fictional creations you probably would and should run screaming from in real life, but on the page, she’s a pretty great hang: spiky, sharp-witted, blazingly self-aware … Hughes has a canny, lyrical ear for her misfits and underdogs, and a touch tender enough to nudge their fate toward better things.”

5. The Key Biscayne Affair by Xita Rubert
(Ecco)

5 Rave • 2 Positive
Read an excerpt from The Key Biscayne Affair here

“Sly, rewarding … Throughout this slender novel, Rubert’s style offers a welcome respite from the minimalism which attenuates so much contemporary fiction. Her sentences are audacious, on tiptoe and reaching. There are wisdoms on every page, shimmering like silica in the sidewalk.”
